title: Biden v. Nebraska (2023)
summary: The HEROES Act's power to waive or modify student loan provisions does not authorize the Secretary of Education to cancel about $430 billion in student debt.
notes:
Key line: "The question here is not whether something should be done; it is who has the authority to do it." Chief Justice Roberts, for the Court.

Citation: 600 U.S. 477 (2023).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were President Joseph R. Biden, Jr., Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona and the Department of Education, which adopted the loan forgiveness plan. Respondents were six states: Nebraska, Missouri, Arkansas, Iowa, Kansas and South Carolina. Missouri asserted injury through the Missouri Higher Education Loan Authority (MOHELA), a public corporation created by the state that services federal student loans and earns fees on the accounts it handles. The Government defended the plan under the Higher Education Relief Opportunities for Students Act of 2003 and argued that no state had standing.
sections.Material Facts: Federal student loans total about $1.6 trillion owed by 43 million borrowers. The HEROES Act lets the Secretary waive or modify any statutory or regulatory provision applicable to federal student aid programs as the Secretary deems necessary in connection with a war or other military operation or national emergency, to ensure that affected individuals are not placed in a worse position financially. In August 2022, relying on the COVID-19 national emergency, the Secretary announced a plan to discharge up to $10,000 of federal loans for borrowers with 2020 or 2021 income below $125,000 ($250,000 for households) and up to $20,000 for Pell Grant recipients. The Department estimated the plan would cover 98.5 percent of borrowers, erase the debts of 20 million people and cost roughly $430 billion. MOHELA, which earned $88.9 million in servicing fees in the prior year, would lose an estimated $44 million a year.
sections.Procedural History: The six states sued in the Eastern District of Missouri in September 2022. The District Court dismissed for lack of standing. The Eighth Circuit entered a nationwide injunction pending appeal, concluding that Missouri likely had standing through MOHELA. The Secretary asked the Supreme Court to vacate the injunction or grant certiorari before judgment. The Court granted certiorari before judgment, heard expedited argument on February 28, 2023, and on June 30, 2023 reversed the dismissal and remanded.
sections.Issue: The HEROES Act lets the Secretary of Education waive or modify statutory provisions governing federal student aid as he deems necessary in connection with a national emergency so that affected individuals are not placed in a worse financial position. Relying on that language and the COVID-19 emergency, the Secretary announced a program cancelling debt for nearly every borrower. Does at least one of the six plaintiff states have Article III standing to challenge the plan, and does the HEROES Act's waive or modify authority permit the Secretary to establish a program cancelling roughly $430 billion of federal student loan principal?
sections.Holding: Missouri has standing because the plan would cost MOHELA, an instrumentality of the state, about $44 million a year in fees, and harm to MOHELA is harm to Missouri. On the merits, the HEROES Act does not authorize the plan. Waive or modify means to make modest adjustments to existing provisions, not to rewrite the statute and create a new forgiveness program. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts first addressed standing. MOHELA was created by Missouri, performs a public function, and its financial harm from lost servicing fees is an injury in fact traceable to the plan; because the Authority is part of the state, Missouri may sue on that injury, as Arkansas could in Arkansas v. Texas. Turning to the statute, the Court said modify carries a connotation of increment or limitation, as in MCI v. AT&T, and the Secretary's changes were not modest. The plan discharged loans for nearly every borrower regardless of circumstance and replaced the Education Act's narrow forgiveness provisions with a novel program. Waive fared no better: the Secretary did not merely waive a provision but added new eligibility terms, and the Act's past use since 2003 involved limited adjustments such as extending deadlines for service members. The Court then invoked the major questions doctrine. Cancelling $430 billion is a decision of vast economic and political significance; Congress had debated and rejected loan forgiveness bills, and the executive branch had earlier said it lacked this authority. Such a decision requires clear congressional authorization, and the Act's general waiver language did not supply it.

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: The student-loan note illustrates the doctrine alongside an ordinary statutory-authority ground.
topics.lrs-i-major-questions-rationales: Barrett’s contextual account is contrasted with Gorsuch’s nondelegation rationale and Kagan’s textual objection.
topics.lrs-n-standing-state: The state-instrumentality relationship drove the divided standing analysis.

learning.separateOpinions: The vote was 6 to 3. Justice Barrett concurred, defending the major questions doctrine as a tool for reading text in context rather than a substantive canon, and explaining that a reasonable reader would not expect an emergency waiver provision to authorize a program of this magnitude. Justice Kagan dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Jackson. She argued that no state had standing because MOHELA, a legally separate corporation, chose not to sue and Missouri could not borrow its injury, and that the HEROES Act plainly permits the Secretary to waive or modify any provision in an emergency, so the Court had overstepped its role.

additionalTreatments.title: Biden v. Nebraska — standing note
additionalTreatments.summary: The majority recognized Missouri’s standing through injury to MOHELA, while the dissent disputed relying on an absent legally distinct entity.

sections.Parties: Missouri challenged the federal student-debt-relief order. The Missouri Higher Education Loan Authority was the state-created entity whose revenues would be affected.
sections.Material Facts: The relief order would reduce MOHELA’s revenues. MOHELA itself had not joined the suit, making its relationship to Missouri central to the standing disagreement.
sections.Procedural History: The assigned note reports the Supreme Court’s standing ruling. It does not reproduce the full loan-program merits or lower-court history.
sections.Issue: Whether injury to MOHELA could be treated as injury to Missouri even without MOHELA as a party.
sections.Holding: The majority held that Missouri had standing because MOHELA acted as a state instrumentality performing a public function. The dissent would not treat Missouri as the proper claimant for the absent entity’s injury.
sections.Reasoning: The majority connected the authority’s public function to the state’s own interests. The dissent invoked the usual restrictions on litigating another party’s rights and emphasized the harmed entity’s absence. The casebook presents the case as a possible counterexample to more restrictive recent state-standing results, rather than as a general rule that a state may always sue for an affiliated entity.
